title: A State Court Authorized the Security Test, but the Sheriff Said the Contract Was Void
dek: A state court's authorization letter had no power over a county courthouse building, so a sanctioned security test became burglary. Even after every charge was dropped, the arrest record stayed on their files forever — the justice system can pay money, but it cannot restore a clean record.
why: It lays out the fragility of an "authorization contract" more clearly than any exploit: the owner of a building can overturn the entire paper trail, and legal accountability is almost entirely blocked by immunity. Anyone in security outsourcing or on the vendor side of a project should pause here.
who: Physical security testing teams, the legal departments of security services vendors, and anyone who walks in on the strength of a client's authorization letter; also technical founders who want to understand how the game of American judicial immunity actually works.
skip: The first half hour of lock-picking technique and door-access detail is technical trivia; if you're impatient, jump to 35:18 to see the conflict erupt.

points.h: A verbal agreement to authorize is no authorization at all
points.body: The rules document was only 28 pages, which makes it easy to assume the written contract had locked everything down. But Gary says the truly detailed arrangements were almost all negotiated verbally over the phone; if it had all been written down, the contract would have run a hundred pages and no one would have signed it. That compromise planted the mine directly: when they later tested the Dallas County Courthouse, the verbally agreed scope did not cover that building — so procedurally they walked into a building that was "not authorized." The sheriff's later claim that there was "no authorization" had its root not in technology but in a contract that could not cover every spoken conversation.

points.h: The building's owner outranks whatever the authorization letter says
points.body: Before the sheriff arrived they were still confident, because the contract stated in black and white that the state court had authorized it. But the sheriff's only response was: they don't own this courthouse, and I don't care whether you have a contract. Only then did Gary and Justin understand that a building's right of use and its contractual rights are separate; no matter how formal the contract the state court signed, it could not make a door decision on behalf of the county court that owned the building. The mood on the spot went from relaxed to arrest, and they had not even been worried before, because no tester in the industry had ever been prosecuted. This time was different.

points.h: The judge heard the truth as a lie
points.body: The judge told Gary, "You must think I'm stupid" — her reasoning being: if the state government had authorized this test, she, as a state employee, should have known; she didn't know, so it could only be a lie. Gary later said this judge had faced criminals' lies for years and could no longer tell what the truth was. A reasonable but dangerous logic: in a courtroom full of lies, an alibi-style contract looks even more fake. Professional reports and legal process all failed in this scenario.

points.h: Dropping the charges does not erase the record
points.body: On January 30, 2020, all charges were dropped, but both men's criminal records will forever say they were arrested on burglary charges. Justin says they were deprived of their rights without due process — in many American background checks, an arrest record is just as conspicuous as a conviction. A dismissal only means no prosecution; it cannot erase the collateral consequences of that arrest: job hunting, passing through customs, clearing security — this stretch will follow them. The clean record they won by fighting the criminal case was in fact only half won.

points.h: The government refuses to answer for its own mistakes by claiming immunity
points.body: Holding anyone accountable was far harder than they imagined. They wanted to sue the sheriff, the prosecutor and the judge, but the system put up two walls: qualified immunity protects individuals acting in their official duties, and sovereign immunity says you cannot sue the government without the government's consent. The state court dismissed first — because the state government was the defendant; the federal court kicked the case back to the state, and the state dismissed it again. This is not a judge deciding a case; it is a system in which no entry point exists for "the government was wrong." The only thing victims can sue is the office, not the person sitting in it; the sheriff personally does not have to pay a single cent. Judicial checks and balances here became an empty adjective.

points.h: You have to win the judicial lottery just to get a little dignity back
points.body: Almost every wrongful arrest case dies in the same place: over 95% are dismissed because of qualified immunity, and most of the rest end in zero damages or a government win. To get more than fifty thousand dollars in compensation, the odds are like winning the lottery, unless you were wrongly locked up for weeks or even months. Gary and Justin were held only one night, yet their evidence was airtight, and they ultimately got a rare public statement at the arbitration: the question was not whether they would win, but how much they could get. Near trial, the county offered three hundred thousand dollars each, six hundred thousand total, to settle. But for them, that money could not buy back the half a life already written into the record.

terms.def: Protects government workers from being sued over acts performed in their official duties, unless those acts clearly violate the Constitution or the law.
The legal principle that a private party cannot sue the government without the government's own consent.
